# Review

The article makes a two-part claim. First, selection-based learning needs a comparison, not a single score, and a robust comparison over a preference model can supply it. Second, a fixed-weight LLM can build that preference model from a stated purpose and make the comparison. The description also commits the article to the weight-training contrast, the Bitter Lesson and the empirical test. Material in those sections therefore serves a declared commitment and is not a branch.

Most side material earns its place under that claim:

- The AlphaGo Zero/AlphaZero contrast and the gradient-update paragraph set the boundary between selection and direct updates. The definition depends on that boundary.
- The Gödel machine, PRODIGY and EURISKO precedents form the proof–formula–judgment progression. This progression locates where the bet enters. The concession that the Gödel machine "is not rigid" stops the contrast from overclaiming.
- The stochastic-dominance example, the Greco et al. framing and "The analogy has a limit" paragraph supply the robust-comparison premise and bound it. The last of these marks where open-ended work departs from the decision-analysis method.
- The cost ledger, the consistency paragraph, the credit-assignment caveat and the five hazards (including *Weak proposals*) bound the bet or state how it can fail. They limit the main claim rather than compete with it.

One passage is a mild branch: the detailed counter-reading of the Harness Evolution study inside the Bitter Lesson section. The finding records it. It may be worth keeping as a short pointer, but its detail belongs more naturally in the source ingest. No branch clearly calls for removal or rehoming, so the outcome is PASS with one INFO finding.

# Review

The article's strongest claim, stated only from its own commitments, is this: selection-based learning over a readable store needs a robust comparison, not a single score, and a fixed-weight LLM can build the preference model from a stated purpose, make that comparison and decide the cases it leaves open.

The core claim is easy to find. The opening question sets it up, the second and third paragraphs state both halves, and the bet is bolded. The later sections clearly serve it. The worked example makes the comparison concrete. The gradient-training contrast and precedents place the bet as the step after proof and fixed formula. The Bitter Lesson section answers the main objection. The final section says how to test the bet and what would refute it. Each section returns to the bet or to the routing-line example. The article therefore passes.

The opening's shape makes the claim less memorable than it should be. The first numbered point carries a definition, two technical terms, a scope restriction, a novelty disclaimer, a historical precedent and an RL analogy. A second novelty disclaimer then splits the bolded bet from its elaboration. A reader leaves the introduction with the hedges as vivid as the claim. The simplest repair is to cut the precedent, analogy and duplicate disclaimer from the opening, because later sections already carry them, and to keep the comparison claim and the bet adjacent.

The bet also appears in two forms. The precedents section gives the sharper one, which adds the open-case decision and the double-loop label. Aligning the opening with it is a revision target. It does not show that the claim is hidden.

The article mostly keeps its detail in proportion. The routing-line walkthrough is a worked example of a mechanism that the bare definition would leave abstract, and later sections reuse it. The AlphaGo Zero/AlphaZero contrast and the direct-update boundary cases each fix a boundary of the definition in a few sentences. There are two places to compress in place. Both are in the "Proof, formula, judgment" section, where background on precedents and on the decision-analysis method grows past its job. The Gödel machine paragraph gives more source detail than the proof-gating contrast needs. The robust-comparison explanation states the agreement rule and its narrowing effect twice: once through stochastic dominance and once through the preference-model method. One statement of each would teach the mechanism the bet depends on just as well.

The Harness Evolution paragraph is somewhat long. Its concessions do argumentative work against the weights-only rival, so it is recorded only as information.

# Deployment-Time Machine Learning: LLM-Selected Updates Without a Single Score

> **Draft.** The claims and structure of this article may change. Comments
> and counterexamples are welcome on
> [the repository's GitHub Discussions page](https://github.com/zby/commonplace/discussions).

A deployed agent can change how it handles its next task by revising an
instruction its next run will read. Its model weights need not change.
The question is which revisions to keep. If a new instruction prevents
routing errors but adds reading time to every task, can a large language
model (LLM) select an update without reducing both effects to one score?

First, **selection-based learning**—learning through proposed changes
that are evaluated and can be rejected—needs a comparison, not a single
score. The judge need only compare the candidates at hand, including
leaving the system unchanged. One scoring function can supply the
comparison when it captures what matters. Often the stated purpose
permits several ways to weigh the gains and losses. Decision analysis calls that set a **preference model**, and
the comparison is **robust** when every function in the set gives the same
answer. A robust comparison can select changes without anyone choosing one
scalar weighting. The case argued here is the one where the changes are
edits to the system's own readable, addressable store. The process itself is
not new: software teams do it when they maintain handbooks and linters, and
symbolic learners such as PRODIGY ran a fixed-formula version of it in the
1980s. Like reinforcement learning, the term names a process with no
built-in guarantee of improvement.

Second, and this is our empirical bet: **a fixed-weight language model can
supply what the selection step needs. It can build the preference model
from a stated purpose and make the robust comparison.** The loop itself is not new. The bet is that the model can identify which
trade-offs the purpose permits, trace later failures to specific edits,
and revise the criteria it uses to judge future edits. Whether spending
more computation on that work yields better decisions is a further test.

## One change followed through

Before stating the paradigm abstractly, follow a single edit through a
deployed agent system that maintains its own knowledge base and instruction
files.

Suppose agents repeatedly misfile design proposals in the wrong directory.
A change is proposed: add one routing line to the main instruction file
loaded on every task, directing design proposals to the right folder and to
the spec that says how a design proposal must be written. A judge evaluates
the proposed edit before it enters the
store. It weighs the expected routing fix against a diffuse cost—every
unrelated task also loads that extra line, and on a task already near the
model's effective context limit, extra prompt text can tip a correct answer
into rework. The judge compares leaving the file alone, adding the line as proposed,
and adding it on trial. It selects the trial: it installs the line and
schedules a review of the next maintenance run. The reviewer will inspect
where the line sent each task and decide whether to keep, narrow, or remove
it. The line takes effect now under either form of adoption; only the trial
also changes what the reviewer will do.

On later tasks, the new line directs proposal writes accurately—until a
longer maintenance run fails because the rule matched a migration plan that
belonged instead in a
[workshop](../theory/a-functioning-kb-needs-a-workshop-layer-not-just-a-library.md),
the system's temporary area for unfinished work. At the scheduled review, the reviewer traces the misfiling to the new line
and narrows its scope to
finished design proposals while leaving the rest of the instruction file
intact. Later still, after three similar over-broad rules pass the system's
existing brevity check, a third change revises the review check itself so
every new routing rule must declare what it excludes before acceptance.

That sequence establishes three things. First, the system adapted across
tasks at deployment time without changing a single model weight: the unit
of learning is [the deployed system, not the model alone](../theory/the-deployed-system-not-the-model-is-the-unit-of-learning.md).
Second, the judge selected the line with a review commitment, not the line
as originally proposed. Whether later work was better with the line
than without it was a separate question. Third, no
single scalar metric had to be invented to compare saved misfilings against
diffuse context load.

## Selection-based learning versus direct gradient training

Our knowledge base defines
[selection-based learning](../theory/definitions/selection-based-learning.md) by
one condition: a change to what the system retains for its later work is
proposed, evaluated, and can be rejected. Evaluation need not be a
separate stage or actor, but its result decides whether the change is made
or undone, and a rejection is its own event. It can apply one
fixed measure, such as a validator or a utility formula, or a comparison
across several.

[AlphaGo Zero](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24270) is a well-known
case. Each newly trained network played the current best one and replaced
it only if it won by a margin of 55%. Its successor
[AlphaZero](../sources/alphazero-chess-shogi-self-play.ingest.md) dropped that step and updated
a single network continually, so it no longer selected among networks.

The gradient steps that trained each network were not selected in either
system. They are direct updates: the evidence determines the change, and
nothing is proposed or rejected. Pre-training by gradient descent works the
same way. It is told the right output for each input, and the error fixes
the update. Automatic trace logging and triggers that write on a count are
direct updates too.

The definition does not say where the retained information is held or who does the
selecting. A deployed checkpoint, a team's working habits, and an
instruction file all qualify. Naming a system adds two questions. The
system is a
[self-improving system](../theory/definitions/self-improving-system.md)
when the selecting is done inside it, and it is double-loop when it can
also revise what it selects by. A model whose checkpoint is picked by its
engineers learns by selection without being self-improving. Commonplace,
our agent-operated knowledge-base framework, does all three today only with
people inside the system. The bet of this article is that the software
alone can, given a stated purpose.

This article treats one case: a readable store, edited by selected changes.
Writing rules down does not change the kind of learning. It gives rules
that an evaluator can read and a later edit can correct one at a time. The
table compares that case with gradient training.

| Axis | Direct gradient training | Selection-based learning over a readable store |
|---|---|---|
| **Modifiable substrate** | Opaque numerical parameters | Readable, [addressable](../theory/definitions/addressable-theory.md) store (prose, structured text, code) |
| **Role of the value / loss function** | Scalar loss, reward, or value function | Rejectable judgment in the loop—from one fixed measure up to a robust comparison across a preference model |
| **When updates happen** | Training or fine-tuning runs | Deployment time, taking effect on the next task that reads the store |
| **Credit assignment and correction** | Backpropagation or policy gradients across parameters | Inspecting traces to edit, narrow, or revert specific entries while keeping the rest |
| **Inspectability** | Requires interpretability probes over weights | Direct reading, diffing, testing, and version control by people or agents |

The last three rows are payoffs of a readable store, and two carry limits.
"Deployment time" places a change in the lifecycle, not its speed:
proposing, evaluating, and safely installing it still take time
([persistent deployment-time adaptation](../theory/retained-artifacts-enable-persistent-deployment-time-adaptation.md)).
Direct reading—by people or by other agents at volumes people could not
read—works only while each rule stays readable at an affordable cost; large
or obscure artifacts can block it
([inspection needs an affordable route, not just readable form](../theory/inspectable-artifact-not-supervision-defeats-the-blackbox-problem.md)).

Those payoffs carry real costs that belong on the ledger of any comparison
with weight training. Explicit artifacts need retrieval, applicability
checks, validation, and ongoing upkeep; a false abstraction in a shared
instruction can misdirect many tasks, while a right rule that retrieval
misses does nothing. Worse, legibility does not guarantee faithfulness:
a plausible written rule need not be what actually drove the model's
behavior, so a rationale read from it can send repair to the wrong rule
([revision guided by rationale needs faithfulness, not just legibility](../theory/revision-guided-by-rationale-needs-faithfulness-not-just-legibility.md)).
Keeping episode records alongside distilled rules preserves a path to
re-examine a rule that goes stale
([retaining episode evidence](../theory/retaining-episode-evidence-keeps-a-distilled-rule-open-to.md)),
at the cost of storing and managing more state.

## Proof, formula, judgment: where the bet enters

If selection-based learning over readable stores is not new, why did earlier
AI systems not turn it into a general machine learning paradigm? The three
precedents raise the same question: how does a system decide whether a
proposed change is worth keeping?

**Formal proof.** Jürgen Schmidhuber's
[Gödel machine](../theory/goedel-machines-are-a-proof-governed-case-of-self-modification.md)
represents the hard-oracle extreme. Its entire software—including its proof
searcher and utility representation—is readable, modifiable code, and live
observations enter proofs on the fly. Yet its admission route lets a
self-rewrite take effect only through a formal proof that switching has
higher expected utility than continuing the current search, under axioms
describing the hardware, environment, and utility. That buys an optimality
guarantee conditional on those axioms and that utility, at a steep price:
the machine must ignore every useful improvement it cannot prove, and a
valid proof does not establish that the axioms adequately describe the
real-world domain—under an inadequate formalization, a proved switch need
not deliver what its user wanted. The machine is not rigid. It can rewrite
even its own utility function when it proves the rewrite better under the
current one. Its limits are which proofs can be found and whether the
formalization is adequate.

**Fixed formula.** Steven Minton's
[PRODIGY](../sources/minton-utility-of-ebl-aaai88.ingest.md) built a
working symbolic selection-based learner in 1988. It kept search-control rules
only while a fixed utility formula estimated positive time saved, updated
each rule's estimate from later use, and dropped rules whose estimate
turned negative. That is genuine **targeted correction**—pinning a loss on
one retained rule and removing it while keeping the rest. What PRODIGY
could not do was question whether its single formula in one unit (time
saved) captured what mattered; it was **single-loop**, needing Minton
outside the system to revise the formula.

**Changing heuristics.** Douglas Lenat's
[EURISKO](../sources/eurisko-learns-new-heuristics-and-domain-concepts.ingest.md),
an early-1980s symbolic program that discovered new heuristics and domain
concepts,
demonstrated the next step—**double-loop** criterion revision. In one
reported episode, after a badly generalized heuristic wasted effort,
EURISKO did not merely drop that heuristic; it also retained a restriction
penalizing future generalizations of that shape before they ran. Changing
what governs later decisions of a class revises the working criterion.
EURISKO could revise its own heuristics, but it still needed Lenat to
correct some judgments of worth. A heuristic could gain credit by
influencing how credit was awarded, not by helping solve the task. Lenat
could reject it on that ground without having to specify a better scoring
formula.

**Robust comparison.** In real engineering and knowledge work, gains and
losses fall on different tasks, and many different scalar value functions
can be defended from the same declared goal. The rule for this case is old and
standard: rank two options only where every admissible value function
agrees. Stochastic dominance is a familiar instance. One gamble dominates
another when every increasing utility function prefers it, and restricting
the set to risk-averse utilities orders more pairs. Multiple-criteria
decision analysis states the rule in the terms used here
([Greco, Mousseau and Słowiński](../sources/greco-ordinal-regression-revisited.ingest.md)).
It keeps every value function compatible with the preferences a person has
stated, and calls that set the preference model. A preference for one
option over another is *necessary* when every function in the set gives it,
and *possible* when at least one does. With no stated preferences, an option
is necessarily preferred only when it is at least as good on every
criterion, which leaves most real changes unordered. Each stated preference
removes functions from the set, so more pairs become ordered. When one
function is left, the method is ordinary selection by a value function.

The analogy has a limit. In that method the criteria are fixed, so each
stated preference can only narrow the set. In open-ended work an objection
can introduce a criterion nobody had listed. That widens the set and can
overturn an earlier verdict.

A
[robust comparison](../theory/necessary-preference-can-guide-improvement-without-a-global-measure.md)
applies this to a change. Once the alternative, the parties whose costs
count, and the horizon are fixed, the change is an improvement when every
compatible value function favors it. This is stricter than the method's
own relation, which asks only that an option be at least as good. When compatible value functions pull
in opposite directions or evidence has not yet arrived, the comparison stays
open—and the system can still act as a bounded decision, using
[reversibility to limit future loss](../theory/reversibility-can-favor-a-change-by-limiting-future-loss.md),
as in the routing-line example above.

In the decision-analysis method, a person states the preferences. **We bet
that a fixed-weight language model can do that work autonomously: derive
the preference model from the declared purpose of the work, make the robust
comparison, and decide the cases it leaves open.** This is double-loop
selection-based learning with targeted correction, for work where no fixed
criterion is adequate. It requires the model not only to compare proposed
edits and diagnose which retained edit caused a later failure, but also to
recognize when an existing gate, validator, or review criterion is
misleading and revise it—while the declared objective the criteria serve
stays fixed
([revising an improvement objective](../theory/revising-an-improvement-objective-is-licensed-from-outside-it.md)).

The bet is not that the model writes down value functions and computes
which option wins under all of them, as the decision-analysis method does.
It is that the model can give reasons that do the same work: which work
changed, whose costs count, and which weighting or observation would
reverse the choice. Those reasons can be checked and challenged one at a
time.

The procedure need not assign every version a number. For the pair at
hand, the judge can favor either version or leave the comparison open.
This says what the judge must do, not how its weights produce an answer.
Even consistent answers can neglect a cost the stated purpose requires
the judge to count. Some open comparisons close when
the alternative is changed. Keeping the routing line for good may be open,
while trying it with a cheap way back can be better under every compatible
measure. What still remains is taken as a decision with its reasons, not
reported as an improvement, and later evidence can reverse it.

Consistency is part of the bet. A model that approves a change and then
approves its reversal on the same evidence is equivalent to no set of value
functions, and such cycles are something a test can look for.

## Compatible with the Bitter Lesson

For many machine learning researchers, the immediate objection is Rich
Sutton's
[Bitter Lesson](http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html):
general methods that leverage computation through search and learning
eventually beat methods built on human domain knowledge. A common folk
reading compresses that into *structure loses to weights*, treating any
system that learns by editing prose or code as a throwback to hand-crafted
symbolic AI.

That folk reading confuses **production method** with **representational
form**
([the Bitter Lesson selects production methods, not representational forms](../theory/the-bitter-lesson-selects-production-methods-not-representational.md)).
The Bitter Lesson contrasts human-supplied knowledge with knowledge
produced by computation through search and learning; it says nothing about
whether the retained result must live in floating-point weights. Scale
displaced hand-tuned weights as well as hand-written features—what lost
spanned both forms because what decided the outcome was how the content was
made.

Sutton himself leans toward the weights-only view: in a 2026
[interview](https://sequoiacap.com/podcast/rich-sutton-and-khurram-javed-why-ai-models-stop-learning-and-how-to-start-it-again),
he and Khurram Javed argue that forming new concepts requires continual
weight updating. That is a substantive rival hypothesis, not a corollary of
the Bitter Lesson essay. A 2026 empirical study,
[Harness Evolution Hits a Ceiling](../sources/harness-evolution-ceiling-weight-training.ingest.md),
reached a similar conclusion after an automated harness-evolution loop
stalled and deferred hard failures to weight training. Yet the authors'
own diagnosis attributed the stall to what the proposer was not shown (its
scorer saw a failure mode in a quarter of runs that never reached the
proposer), though their single remedy run stayed within noise. On one model
line the whole harness gain came from editing a natural-language lessons
file.

Once a language model supplies the comparison inside an automated
selection loop, the system sits on the computation side of the Bitter
Lesson. Additional compute can be spent on more candidate proposals,
richer execution traces, independent criticism, targeted revisions, and
revised working criteria—all automatically generated and tested rather
than hand-authored. Whether that spending pays as the store grows is open.
The hard problem is credit assignment without a chain rule: when entries
depend on each other, a later failure rarely identifies which entry should
change.

One strict condition attaches. A system bootstrapped from hand-written
instructions, types, and review gates—as Commonplace currently is—fits the
Bitter Lesson
[only if automated learning outgrows that starting point](../theory/a-bootstrap-fits-the-bitter-lesson-only-if-learning-outgrows-it.md).

## Whether a change improved the system, current evidence, and limits

Because selection-based learning names a process with no success
condition, the paradigm claim stays honest only if success is judged
separately. A change is an event, and what the store keeps is
content. So the comparison is between two states of the system that differ
only in what the change did, whether it added, revised or removed content,
with entries that depend on it adjusted to match. The change improved the
system when the state that has its effect is robustly better at its later
work: better under every compatible measure of the declared work over the
declared horizon.

For a recent edit—like our routing line on the day it is added—the verdict
is normally **open** until later episodes arrive. Passing the check that
admitted an edit does not show that later work is better.
Letting a change stand while its verdict is open is a decision, not a
demonstrated gain.

Testing the bet therefore requires a two-part empirical check on fresh
tasks outside the episode that prompted the edit:

1. **Operative dependence.** Withholding or altering the retained entry
   must change later behavior
   ([operative change](../theory/definitions/operative-change.md)). Loading
   a memory file on every run proves nothing if the model ignores it.
2. **Robust improvement.** The changed behavior must score higher under
   every compatible measure of the declared work, not merely pass the
   check that admitted it.

Honest sets of compatible measures leave many trade-offs open. A test
therefore reports an open comparison as open, and is built around contrasts
clean enough to resolve.
[Testing Autonomous Selection-Based Learning](./testing-autonomous-selection-based-learning.md)
sets those comparisons out.

**Current state of evidence.** Commonplace is an active, human-assisted
bootstrap developing the store, review machinery, and judgment probes. We
report **no completed end-to-end automated run** demonstrating sustained
autonomous double-loop learning yet.

**Material limits and failure modes.** Even if the loop runs without human
intervention, five hazards can defeat it:

- *Judgment reliability.* Language-model judges can miss diffuse costs,
  hallucinate causal links in traces, or approve plausible-sounding edits
  that fail in practice.
- *False-positive retention.* Unlike proof-gated switches, empirical
  admission admits harmful changes, and
  [false-positive acceptance becomes operative](../theory/false-positive-generation-is-filtered-before-retention.md)
  until later evidence catches it.
- *Unfaithful rationales.* Legible prose can diverge from what actually
  steers the model's outputs, masking the real cause of gains or losses.
- *Accretion and maintenance drag.* Local gains are salient while context
  load and rule interactions are diffuse, so a chain of locally plausible
  edits can degrade aggregate performance unless whole-store comparisons
  and pruning counteract it.
- *Weak proposals.* A comparison selects only among the candidates that
  search reaches. A sound judge over poor proposals still learns little,
  and the bet stated here is about the comparison, not about how good the
  proposals are.

If controlled runs show that automated language-model judgment cannot keep
false-positive acceptance, unfaithful rationales, and accretion below the
gains it finds, the bet fails—and those domains stay with weights-only
continual learning or with engineering governed by people.

## Where to go next

- [Testing Autonomous Selection-Based Learning](./testing-autonomous-selection-based-learning.md)
  — the comparisons that would test the bet, and a proposed first
  experiment.
- [The definition](../theory/definitions/selection-based-learning.md) —
  the full definition, including what a claim must name and boundary cases
  such as triggers and direct updates. A companion definition covers
  [single-loop and double-loop learning](../theory/definitions/single-loop-and-double-loop-learning.md).
- [Necessary preference can guide improvement without a global measure](../theory/necessary-preference-can-guide-improvement-without-a-global-measure.md)
  — what a claim of improvement asserts, how to decide when the comparison
  is open,
  and Commonplace's declared objective; paired with
  [reversibility can favor a change by limiting future loss](../theory/reversibility-can-favor-a-change-by-limiting-future-loss.md).
- Companion drafts in this collection—written before this framing
  was adopted and currently being re-anchored from the narrower *theory
  builder* special case (where the store holds explicit, criticized
  theories):
  [Testing Whether a Theory Builder Learns](./testing-whether-a-theory-builder-learns.md),
  [Bootstrapping an Autonomous Theory Builder with Commonplace](./bootstrapping-an-autonomous-theory-builder.md),
  and
  [Which Existing Self-Improving Systems Are Theory Builders](./which-existing-self-improving-systems-are-theory-builders.md).

---
description: "Synthesize a compression review into at most three high-level simplifications that materially improve the artifact but still require authorial judgment"
type: types/instruction.md
depth: 4

# Synthesize high-impact simplification opportunities

Read the complete artifact and the individual compression findings. Report only opportunities likely to materially improve a reader's understanding of the central claim, conceptual structure, or argumentative flow. Do not edit the artifact.

An opportunity qualifies when its benefit would be large but its implementation requires broader judgment. Typical cases include surfacing a buried thesis, making the role of a load-bearing paragraph explicit, combining several local findings into one deletion or fold, or reorganizing an explanation whose current sequence hides the argument. Exclude local wording improvements, cosmetic changes, minor compression, and alternatives that are merely different.

The synthesis may combine several gate findings or identify a global reorganization visible only after reading the artifact as a whole. Ground every opportunity in the artifact or the gate findings; do not invent a stronger thesis for the artifact to serve.

Distinguish a buried contribution from an undetermined one. A contribution supported by the artifact can be surfaced or given a clearer role. If the artifact does not select among materially different theses, audiences, or purposes, report the missing choice under `Preserve or decide`; do not choose one merely to make the prose cohere. This isolated synthesis receives no retained-intent input, so do not import the choice from the topic, a bare writing prompt, or ambient conversation. The calling workflow may later resolve it from explicit user direction or a separate memory input. A [bare writing prompt does not determine its intended contribution](../../theory/a-bare-writing-prompt-does-not-determine-its-intended-contribution.md).

If the simplification depends on choosing among materially different meanings, conceptual roles, evidence claims, or substantive conclusions, name that unresolved choice as a prerequisite. Do not resolve it as a compression edit. Semantic gates or the author must settle it first.

Return zero to three opportunities. For each one, give:

- the location and smallest useful quotation or section range;
- the important reader problem;
- the direction a revision could take;
- the compression findings it combines, if any; and
- the meanings, implications, or structural choices the author must resolve or preserve.

Do not present a rewrite as settled. A short candidate formulation may illustrate the opportunity, but label it as one possible resolution. Keep fact-checking, claim evaluation, and general completeness review outside this synthesis unless they are necessary to explain why the simplification cannot safely proceed.

## Running it alone

The [compression bundle](../run-compression-bundle-on-note.md) applies this synthesis after its four checks, under the bundle's own output contract. The inputs and output below apply when the synthesis runs alone.

### Inputs

The compression findings are explicit input files, one per check, such as the four check results under `kb/reports/state/review/results/<note-path>/`. Run the synthesis alone:

```bash
commonplace-review NOTE --criteria compression-synthesis \
  --input core-claim-obscured=PATH --input branch-bloat=PATH \
  --input detail-overhang=PATH --input marginal-value-redundancy=PATH
```

Use only the supplied findings. Do not run a check, and do not look for other findings. The run keeps its result as a retained observation and writes no current result, because no freshness hash covers the supplied findings.

### Output

The caller names the output file. Write only that file; mutate nothing else. The output is a [review result](../../types/review-result.md) fragment with `outcome: report` and no `attack-outcome`. Each opportunity is one finding, zero to three in all. Give it `scope: passage` with its smallest useful quotation, or `scope: document` with no quotes for a section range or a cross-cutting change. Its `reason` states the reader problem and the direction.

```markdown
---
type: types/review-result.md
findings:
  - scope: passage
    quotes: ["<smallest useful quotation>"]
    reason: "<reader problem>; <direction a revision could take>"
outcome: report
---

# Simplification synthesis: <note title>

## Opportunities

### 1. <short opportunity name>

- Location: <heading and quotation or section range>
- Combines: <the compression findings, or "cross-cutting">
- Preserve or decide: <meanings, implications or structural choices the author must resolve or preserve>
```

Write `None` under `## Opportunities` when no opportunity clears the threshold.

type: types/type-spec.md
name: review-result
description: "One completed gate, conformance or report-method assessment with structured findings and controller-owned execution provenance"
schema: ./review-result.schema.yaml
---

# Review result

A review result records one assessment of captured target text against a criterion. Completion means the output passed deterministic checks, not that its judgment is correct. A report outcome is not a favorable verdict. Use this type for individual gate, compression-check, type-conformance and collection-conformance verdicts, and for critique, composition-friction, premise-decomposition and compression-synthesis reports and role reports. Do not use it for combined improvement packets or connection discovery.

## Content

Findings state what the assessed text establishes or fails to establish. Each passage finding quotes enough verbatim text to identify one contiguous span uniquely. A quote is matched after whitespace and typographic quote marks are normalized, so a line wrap in the target does not break it. A quote therefore identifies a passage and is not a byte-exact copy of it. A consumer that needs the exact span locates the quote in the captured target, which holds the exact bytes. A document-wide or absence finding explains the condition without inventing a quotation. Finding levels belong to verdict criteria; critique reports instead state whether the strongest attack lands and how the note engages it. An empty findings list is an honest completed result when no finding remains.

The body explains the assessment without repeating every structured finding. A critique preserves its central commitment, critique mode, strongest case, the note's response and constructive findings, including why an attack does not survive. Low-confidence no-surviving-attack findings leave the need for a domain check visible.

Each report method has its own shape, which the schema checks by the result's `criterion`:

| Method | Findings | Required body |
|---|---|---|
| Critique | constructive findings | `attack-outcome` in frontmatter; `## Strongest case against it`, `## How the note engages it`, `## Constructive findings` |
| Composition friction | the surfaced joints, thinnest first; each reason begins `UNSUPPORTED`, `THIN` or `HOLDS` | a `**Filter:** SURVIVES` or `DISSOLVES` line; `## Filter`, `## Thinnest joints`, `## For the human` |
| Premise decomposition | one per premise; each reason begins `HOLDS`, `DOUBTFUL` or `DEFEATED`, and a non-`HOLDS` reason names `LOCAL` or `GLOBAL` and `instance`, `prevalence` or `priced-exception` | a `**Register:**` line; `## Premises and counterexamples`, `## For the human` |
| Compression synthesis | zero to three opportunities | `## Opportunities` |
| Role report | one per dependent need, duplication or untaken recommendation; each reason begins `SUPPLIED`, `PARTLY SUPPLIED`, `NOT SUPPLIED`, `DUPLICATED` or `UNTAKEN` | `## Role`, `## Dependents`, `## Duplication`, `## Untaken recommendations`, `## Reach` |

Only critique supplies `attack-outcome`. Friction's filter line and the premise statuses route attention; they are not overall verdicts. A report criterion is named by its library instruction's identity, so moving one of these instructions requires a schema edit.

## Field ownership

The worker fragment supplies only `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, optional `attack-outcome`, and the body. Findings precede the outcome so the serialized verdict follows its rationale. The fragment is not a complete saved artifact. The controller completes and validates it; workers never assert hashes, execution identities or timestamps.

| Fields | Owner and meaning |
|---|---|
| `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, `attack-outcome` | Worker assessment; findings contain `scope`, `quotes`, `reason`, and `level` for verdicts |
| `description`, `format`, `contract` | Controller's result-format identity and expected verdict/report contract |
| `note`, `criterion` | Original target and criterion identities |
| `note-sha256`, `criterion-sha256` | Freshness hashes; the note hash may cover normalized watched parts, not exact bytes |
| `target-sha256`, `target-capture` | Exact assessed UTF-8 bytes and their retained repository-relative location |
| `observation`, `contract-sha256` | Execution observation and captured output-contract identity |
| `profile`, `model`, `run`, `launch`, `completed-at` | Requested execution configuration and observed execution provenance |
| `raw-output`, `raw-output-sha256` | Retained original worker fragment, distinct from this completed artifact |

## Template

Worker fragment for a verdict criterion; code supplies the remaining fields:

```markdown
---
type: types/review-result.md
findings:
  - scope: document
    quotes: []
    reason: "The claim omits the condition needed for its stated conclusion."
    level: warn
outcome: warn
---

# Review

## Summary

The conclusion needs its missing condition.
```

A critique fragment uses `outcome: report`, supplies `attack-outcome`, and omits finding levels. Its body retains the critique instruction's sections. Other report fragments use `outcome: report`, omit `attack-outcome` and finding levels, and follow their instruction's Output section. Neither fragment uses a terminal `## Result:` line. Operational production and publication belong to the review command, not to this type.

# Writing conventions for kb/reports/ (report collection)

## Purpose and scope

This collection contains analytical outputs, evaluation records, and local
operational evidence that are consumed as reports rather than as library
claims or system definitions. Placement here is justified by the output's
retention policy and consumer, not by its filename or by the fact that a tool
generated it.

A report belongs here only when a named operation consumes the report itself.
Transferable claims belong in `kb/theory/`; descriptions of the shipped system
and its decisions belong in `kb/reference/`; executable procedures belong in
`kb/instructions/`; and reasoning whose value is consumed by unfinished work
belongs in `kb/work/`.

## Policy areas

Every report artifact lives in exactly one first-level policy area:

| Area | Retention policy | Typical contents |
|---|---|---|
| `state/` | Ignored, one directory per producing workflow. Not disposable merely because it was generated: the owning workflow decides when an output may be removed, and the [state README](./state/README.md) states per workflow what deletion loses. | Review results, packets and runs; fix dispositions; ingest working directories; connect, critique, friction, premise-decomposition and promotion-candidate reports. |
| `retained/` | Durable report records kept with the project. Payloads are tracked. | Evaluation corpora, experiment reports, measurements, and exact records cited by later work. |
| `types/` | Collection-local structural contracts, not report payloads. | Optional project-authored report contracts; command-produced generic report types are global. |

The published site includes `retained/` and leaves out `state/`. Inside `retained/`, a subtree carrying a
`.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker is left out of the site as well as
validation; mark exact captures and trial bundles so, keeping the report that
interprets them published.

Do not put report payloads directly at the collection root. Moving an artifact
between policy areas is a change in its retention contract, not a filing-only
rename.

## Quality goal

Make the report sufficient for the operation that consumes it without making
it impersonate a durable knowledge claim. State the subject, inputs or source
state, method, result, and material limits to the degree needed to interpret
or reproduce the output. Record the model and prompt or instruction identity
when an LLM judgment is part of the evidence and the producing workflow does
not already retain them.

`state/` must satisfy the owning workflow's authority, integrity, and cleanup
rules. `retained/` must remain
understandable from a clean checkout without relying on ignored files.

## Titles, descriptions, and exact records

- Use a title that names the analysis, experiment, or result. A title such as
  "Report" does not distinguish the artifact.
- When frontmatter is present, write a retrieval-oriented `description` that
  identifies the subject and why the exact output is retained.
- Frontmatter-free Markdown is permitted for deliberate unstructured output.
- Preserve an exact capture when fidelity is the report's purpose. If a copied
  artifact carries another collection's local type only as captured data, put
  a `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at the capture-set root rather than
  presenting that copy as a live typed artifact of this collection.

## Maintenance semantics

- A state producer owns cleanup and states, in the state README, what deleting
  its output loses: nothing unique (rebuild from retained inputs), one paid
  judgment (rerun when needed) or current coverage, an unresolved disposition
  or decision evidence (preserve). Generated state may contain non-reproducible
  judgments or the only current disposition, so Git ignore status never
  licenses deletion.
- A retained report is changed according to its declared role. Correct a
  living report in place; preserve a dated or frozen observation as an exact
  record and create a new observation when the measured state changes.
- Local evidence notes are the one interpreted form `retained/` keeps as
  durable artifacts: a `types/note.md` artifact whose bounded inference
  concerns only Commonplace's own choices or their measured effects, beside
  the raw records it interprets. Its formal edges use this collection's labels
  below. An inference that keeps a free variable belongs in
  `kb/theory/evidence/`.
- If a report develops a transferable claim, binding rule, system premise, or
  unfinished-work lifecycle, extract that content to its proper collection.
  Do not broaden `retained/` into a second notes, reference, instructions, or
  workshop collection.

## Outbound links

Reports may inspect any project surface. Use relative Markdown links for live
navigation and state in prose why the target matters. Inline links may carry
ordinary evidential or procedural context. Footer-shaped formal edges use this
small authorized set:

| label | destinations | reader need |
|---|---|---|
| `derived-from` | sources, external | inspect the source material from which the report was produced |
| `is-evidence-for` | theory, reference, reports | inspect the durable claim, decision, or report record on which this output bears |
| `compares-with` | theory, reference, sources, reports | compare two artifacts on a named shared axis |
| `see-also` | any durable collection, external | inspect useful adjacent context when no stronger relation applies |

The destination collection separately decides whether it may author a
reciprocal edge. A formal edge into this collection targets `retained/`;
`state/` may be mentioned inline only as local operational context.

Tracked library artifacts must not depend on an ignored `state/` file being
present. Summarize the needed evidence in the tracked artifact or
promote the exact report to `retained/` first. Tracked artifacts may cite a
`retained/` report when the exact record is useful to their reader.

## Validation markers

The tracked `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at `state/` excludes its
data-bearing subtree from collection-scoped validation. The marker does not
hide files from ordinary discovery, and explicit validation of
one typed report still applies its type contract.

A file under `state/` may declare any valid type spec, including another
collection's local type. Workflows stage candidates there for other
collections, and a candidate must validate against its destination's contract.
The type spec itself stays in the owning collection's `types/` directory.
`retained/` does not share this exception.

## What does not belong here

- A generated explanation or synthesis whose claim should survive the run →
  `kb/theory/` or `kb/reference/` according to its consumer.
- A procedure named "report" because it produces one → `kb/instructions/`.
- Drafts, deliberation, and run traces consumed by an unfinished investigation
  → `kb/work/`.
- External source captures and their durable analyses → `kb/sources/`.
- Build outputs with no report consumer → their build cache, not `kb/reports/`.
